Furthermore, in order to give consideration to the dynamic response of the DC side, the two-port circuit model of voltage source converter (VSC) is built by making use of the unified energy path theory and the concept of energy hub. Next, on the basis of the system topology, the circuit model of AC/DC hybrid system can be acquired, which provides a reliable method for the problem of low-frequency oscillation in high-permeability new energy grid connection. More importantly, topology and circuit theory/method can be employed to investigate the dynamic response characteristics of AC/DC side interfaces under different types of disturbances, without constructing complex differential equations. Finally, the validity of the proposed modeling method is proved by building the MATLAB/Simulink model and physical experiment.

title: Equivalent Inertia Mechanism Modeling and Magnitude-Phase Characteristics Analysis of Grid-Supporting MMC-HVDC Systems
abstract: The grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems emulate synchronous generator characteristics to enable efficient power transmission while providing frequency support. However, existing studies lack analytical insights into the equivalent inertia and time-varying supporting mechanism under different control strategies. To address this, an equivalent inertia analytical model for grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems is firstly established from a frequency-domain perspective. The proposed models can accurately describe the equivalent inertia and the time-varying characteristics under different control modes, and their validity and correctness are verified through comparative simulation case studies. Based on the established model, the magnitude-phase supporting characteristics of grid-supporting MMC-HVDC are analyzed. The amplitude |HMMC(s)| is derived to evaluate the magnitude of inertia support capability provided by the MMC-HVDC, while the resonance frequency ωpeak is employed to analyze the phase-delay characteristics of the maximum inertia supporting power and the influence on frequency recovery. Besides, the supporting mechanism of different parameters on the equivalent inertia are analyzed, and the dominant characteristics of these parameters during different stages of frequency recovery is revealed. Simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed model and conclusions.

title: Discharge-Induced Surface Electrode Degradation in Metallized Film Capacitors: A Comparison Under AC and DC Conditions for UHVDC Applications
abstract: Metallized film capacitors (MFCs) are widely used for DC voltage stabilization and AC harmonic filtering in converter stations of UHVDC systems. However, the growing demand for higher voltage and miniaturization poses challenges to the operating reliability of MFCs. This study employs adaptive signal decomposition denoising and image processing techniques to compare discharge signals and surface electrode degradation of metallized films under DC and AC conditions. A capacitance-reducing discharge (CRD) concept applicable to various operating conditions in converter stations is proposed, encompassing self-healing (SH), flashover around SH points, and margin flashover. Under DC conditions, CRD features high-intensity and more pronounced oscillations. Larger SH points account for 71.2% of capacitance reduction with distinct penetrating flashover paths being observed. Under AC conditions, SH points are smaller and more circular. Frequent flashover discharges cause extensive surface electrode evaporation, with flashover around SH points contributing 40.1% of the overall degradation. The energy of CRD exhibits a power-law relation with the applied voltage, with its exponent factor under DC stress twice that under AC stress. The findings provide theoretical support for the reliability of high-performance MFCs in UHVDC applications.

title: Voltage Regulation Under Prosumer-Grid Conflicts: An Evolutionary Learning Strategy
abstract: The modern power grid experiences significant voltage violations due to evolving spatio-temporal variations in load and photovoltaic (PV) generation patterns. Although distributed energy resources (DERs) at the prosumer end help remedy this problem, prosumers’ profit-seeking decisions may conflict with the distribution system operator’s (DSO) technical concerns of maintaining grid voltages. This conflict makes the decision-making through existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) strategies challenging, which otherwise offer a promising solution for simplistic grid-centric objectives. Therefore, to solve a potential prosumer-grid conflict, the incentive mechanism is introduced for prosumers with a multi-agent evolutionary reinforcement learning (MAERL) approach for robust decision-making. Specifically, a teaming mechanism is devised to help agents explore a large search space and escape local minima, enhancing traditional MADRL capabilities. Additionally, we explicitly integrate two key features for a realistic and scalable solution: 1) a hybrid policy network that is rightly needed for the prosumer’s discrete-continuous actions and 2) a Bayesian neural network (BNN)-based surrogate model for power flow, which is selected particularly because of its scalability edge over its nonparametric counterpart, a Gaussian process regression (GPR) method. For validation and performance demonstration, a modified IEEE 33-bus system is used as a case study.

title: BF-YOLO:GIS Inner Surface Detection Model Based on an Improved YOLOv8
abstract: Gas insulated switchgear (GIS) equipment, a crucial component of power grids, requires regular maintenance to ensure stable operation. However, traditional inspection methods have limitations in detecting internal surface defects in GIS pipes, potentially resulting in inefficiencies and safety risks. This paper proposes BF-YOLO, an improved method for internal surface defect detection based on YOLOv8, to address this challenge. BF-YOLO utilizes ShapeIoU loss to focus on edge shapes and scale, enabling more accurate bounding box regression and enhancing detection precision. The FasterNetBlock module helps reduce the model size for more efficient deployment on embedded devices or mobile platforms. The C2F_Faster module further optimizes parameters and model volume while maintaining detection accuracy. Additionally, the reconstructed neck structure, inspired by BiFPN, expands the model's receptive field and enhances spatial information processing, thereby improving the detection of small targets. Compared to the original YOLO model, BF-YOLO demonstrates significant improvements, with mAP@0.5 increasing by 1.1% while the number of parameters and GFLOPs are reduced by 44.1% and 22.2% respectively. These improvements enable faster and more accurate defect detection in GIS pipelines. BF-YOLO provides a valuable solution for automated defect detection, thereby enabling proactive maintenance and enhancing safety and reliability in power grid operations.

title: Observation and Numerical Calculation of Induced Voltage Caused by M Component on 10 kV Overhead Distribution Line
abstract: This article analyzes the lightning-induced voltage (LIV) waveforms generated by M-components recorded by rocket-triggered lightning experiments and performs numerical calculations to investigate the impact of variations in M-component process parameters on the LIV waveforms. The LIVs were measured on a vertically arranged, 1513-meter-long, 10 kV three-phase overhead distribution line. Based on the occurrence time of the M-component, the characteristics of the current waveform, and the polarity of the induced voltage, the M-components measured can be classified into three Types. In addition, this study employs the method of controlling variables and utilizes the hybrid MTL-PEEC (Multi-Conductor Transmission Line – Partial Element Equivalent Circuit) model to analyze the influence of M-component parameters on the induced voltage. The results indicate that an increase in the current rise time leads to a decrease in the absolute value of the negative peak of the induced voltage at the nearest pole, while the positive peak and polarity reversal time increase. An increase in the current half-width results in a longer polarity reversal time and extended decay time after the positive peak. A higher ground reflection coefficient causes increases in both the negative and positive peaks of the induced voltage. Furthermore, an increase in channel height leads to a greater absolute value of the negative peak, a decrease in the positive peak, and a delay in the time to reach peak voltage.

title: A Uniform Grid-Forming Control of Multi-Terminal DC Systems
abstract: The control of a multi-terminal dc (MTDC) system is challenging due to the flexible control modes of AC-DC converter stations at different terminals. In this paper, a uniform grid-forming control method is proposed, which can be applied to all AC-DC converter stations at all terminals of a MTDC system. It can provide the grid-forming and damping effects, and meanwhile achieve the transfer of these effects among the whole system. The different extension formats of the proposed control method are analyzed. The steady-state power flow and the small-signal stability of the whole MTDC system are comprehensively discussed. The time-domain simulations of a five-terminal dc system with renewable energy generation and energy storage are conducted, to validate the corresponding theoretical analysis.

title: Shaping the Q-U Droop Characteristic of Grid-Forming Converters From the Perspective of Constant Voltage Control
abstract: With the increasing penetration rate of variable renewable energy (VRE) and other inverter-based resources (IBR) in power systems, system inertia and strength are being continuously weakened. Grid-forming (GFM) technology, adaptable to weak grids, has attracted widespread attention. The GFM Q-U droop control is widely adopted in practice, but it is challenging to tune key parameters, such as initial voltage reference value and droop coefficient, therefore, the adaptability and effectiveness of voltage support is difficult to ensure. To take the advantages of GFM converters as voltage sources, adopting constant voltage control (CVC) seems to be a better choice. This paper clarifies the implicit internal connection between CVC and droop control, indicating that the droop characteristic does not inherently depend on droop control, but should be regarded as a natural external port performance under internal CVC. Based on above analysis, a novel shaping method for Q-U droop characteristic of GFM converters from the perspective of CVC using virtual impedance is proposed. The virtual impedance in the proposed method is straightforward to set due to its explicit physical meaning, and the method performs well in strong adaptability and robustness for both islanded and grid-connected modes. Finally, the conclusions and the control effectiveness are verified by theoretical analysis, simulation, and experimental results.

title: A MADRL Driven Optimization Framework for Grid Node Inertia and Grid-Forming Converter Damping Characteristics in Microgrids
abstract: The integration of numerous new energy generators into the AC grid will diminish the inertia characteristics traditionally provided by synchronous generators, leading to frequency instability. The inertia and damping constants of the more widely used grid-forming converter (GFC) control methods are fixed. This paper proposes a multi-intelligent deep learning (MADRL) based optimization strategy to enhance the inertia and damping characteristics of GFCs. We begin by analyzing the constraints of the inertia that GFC source measurements can provide and propose a method for acquiring the inertia time constant (ITC) based on node active power and frequency. This method facilitates the partitioning of the distribution grid according to ITC values. Furthermore, we implement characteristic-enhanced branching to optimize inertia and damping characteristics through MADRL decision-making. Utilizing an IEEE-129 network with multiple new energy field stations, the experimental results demonstrate that this approach can increase the ITC of most nodes by over five times. In addition, we maintain frequency fluctuations within 0.01pu, representing a reduction of more than 95% compared to virtual synchronous generator control, while the maximum frequency transient fluctuation decreases by 81%. Furthermore, through comparative experiments and transfer learning, it can be demonstrated that this method possesses sufficient superiority and plug-and-play capability.

title: Available-Power-Constrained Coordinated Fault Voltage Support Control for Multiple Inverter-Interfaced DGs
abstract: The increasing prevalence of weak grid conditions necessitates that inverter-interfaced distributed generators (IIDGs) support voltage during faults to prevent further disturbances. However, maximizing IIDGs’ voltage support capability while respecting operational constraints to prevent unintended tripping remains challenging. This paper proposes an available-power-constrained coordinated fault voltage support control strategy for multiple IIDGs. First, based on the fault characteristics of resistive-inductive distribution networks (DN), a current reference strategy is developed to maximize each IIDG’s voltage support contribution. Then, considering constraints of non-fault-phase voltage and power fluctuation, the safe operating domain of each IIDG is derived. On this basis, an adaptive fault voltage support control framework is constructed, where a zonal clustering method enables communication free coordinated control among multiple IIDGs. In addition, the applicable condition of the proposed method is quantified using the grid short-circuit ratio (SCR) of the grid. Simulation results show that, for case of SCR lower than 3, the proposed method can improve the fault voltage of DNs by 30.8%.

title: Routing and Scheduling of Mobile Energy Storage Systems for Distribution Network Resilience Enhancement Based on a Hybrid Data-Model Driven Approach
abstract: Mobile Energy Storage Systems (MESSs) are critical for improving distribution network resilience under extreme weather events. However, the mathematical model for MESS routing and scheduling is essentially a high-dimensional mixed-integer nonlinear stochastic optimization problem. To accurately and rapidly obtain the routing and scheduling of MESSs and the optimal operation of distribution networks, a bi-level optimization of MESS routing and scheduling based on a hybrid data-model driven approach is proposed. In the upper level, the data-driven approach is achieved by the graph attention network multi-agent conservative soft actor-critic reinforcement learning (GMARL) to determine optimal routing decisions for MESS in the transportation network while taking into account traffic flow and road repair time uncertainties. The proposed GMARL takes full advantage of a graph attention network for feature extraction, and adopts the multi-agent conservative soft actor-critic to mitigate overestimation caused by out-of-distribution experiences, thereby effectively coordinating multiple MESSs to achieve the optimal strategy. In the lower level, a mixed-integer second-order cone programming is formulated to obtain optimal scheduling strategies for MESSs, reconfiguration and optimal power flow in the distribution network. Upon determining the scheduling strategies and amount of load recovery, the reward function value for each MESS can be calculated and used to update the neural network parameters of GMARL, thereby further optimizing the routing strategies of MESSs. Finally, case studies on an IEEE 33-bus active distribution network and a 12-node transportation network are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Optimal Sizing of Energy Storage Systems for Grid-Forming Wind Turbines in Offshore Wind Farms
Dynamic Interaction Modeling and Stability Analysis for Grid-Connected Renewable Energy Systems With High Inertia Energy Storage Synchronous Condenser
abstract: The high inertia energy storage synchronous condenser (HIESSC), which integrates the doubly-fed machine technology with flywheel energy storage, has recently emerged as a promising means to support both frequency and voltage regulation in renewable energy sources (RESs). Despite its novelty, the impact of the HIESSC on system oscillations and the interactions among the control loops of RES stations remains unclear. This paper examines a grid-connected system comprising the HIESSC and a grid-connected converter with grid-following control (GCC-GFL). Firstly, a single-input-single-output interaction model is developed through equivalent block diagram transformations. By incorporating the grid-side coupling impedance and transfer functions of interacting subsystems, the proposed model reveals how the HIESSC modifies the dynamic characteristics of GCC-GFL through a feedback control perspective. Subsequently, the impact of HIESSC operating modes and operating points on the small-signal stability is analyzed. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed methods and analyses is validated by the experiments.

title: Carbon, Cost and Capacity: Weighted-Objective Charging of Electric Buses
abstract: The public transport sector is in the process of decarbonizing by electrifying its bus fleets. This results in challenges if the high electricity demand resulting from battery charging demand is confronted with limited grid capacity and high synchronicity at bus charging sites. In this paper, we explore weighted-objective scheduling for bus charging sites to minimize the emissions associated with charging processes and to aid the operation of the electricity grid by mitigating peak consumption. In particular, we discuss and validate optimization approaches for those individual objectives, as well as their weighted combination, based on data from a real-life bus charging site in the Netherlands. The simulation results show that compared to uncontrolled charging, power peaks can be reduced by up to 40%, while time-of-use emissions associated with the charging of electric buses are also reduced significantly. Furthermore, by using a baseload recorded at a German industrial site, we illustrate the flexibility potential offered by bus charging sites, and advocate that such sites should share a grid connection with other high-load assets.

title: Privacy-Preserving Coordination of Heterogeneous Electrolyzers: A Federated Reinforcement Learning Approach With Safety Guarantees
abstract: The complementarity between high-flexibility Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) and low-cost Alkaline (ALK) electrolyzers contributes to the synergistic development of green power and hydrogen sectors. However, wide-range renewable power fluctuations impose technical challenges on the optimal power allocation among these heterogeneous PEM and ALK units, which might result in safety violations and operational inefficiency. To address these challenges, this study proposes a privacy-preserving, physics-informed federated multi-agent control framework. Specifically, the architecture leverages a federated learning paradigm to aggregate decentralized strategies with limited direct data exchange, while incorporating an LSTM-enhanced algorithm to resolve partial observability by tracking long-timescale multiphysics dynamics like thermodynamic evolution and gas purity. Furthermore, a dual-tier proactive defense mechanism integrating a robust risk predictor with a quadratic programming projection layer is designed to strictly enforce hard physical constraints. Numerical results verify that the proposed approach effectively balances data privacy, physical safety, and precise regulation performance.

title: A Unified Reliability Modeling Framework for MMC Considering Flexible Submodule Configuration and Preventive Maintenance
abstract: Conventional analytical models for engineering-scale modular multilevel converters (MMCs) face significant challenges in reliability assessment, particularly in incorporating preventive maintenance (PM) and redundancy. This paper proposes a simulation-based reliability modeling approach using the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method, which tracks the system-level operational state evolution while considering PM. The approach enables the determination of reliability indices for engineering-scale systems and identifies the optimal fixed PM intervals and redundancy submodule (SM) configurations. Furthermore, it enables flexible adjustment of both the number and type of SMs within a unified framework for reliability assessment. Based on extensive simulation and validation, the method demonstrates its effectiveness in supporting reliability analysis and system design, offering a general framework for practical applications.

title: Design and Verification of Novel Self-Voltage Sharing Vacuum Interrupter for Multi-Break VCBs in GIS
abstract: A key challenge for multi-break vacuum circuit breakers (VCBs) in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) is the design of compact voltage grading solutions for vacuum interrupters (VIs). This paper addresses the non-uniform voltage distribution across VI shields and series-connected breaks in VCBs that is caused by the significantly increased stray capacitances in GIS. To address these issues, we propose a novel self-voltage sharing capacitor pattern (SSCP), and the equivalent circuit of the VI with SSCP is analyzed. Simulations of the SSCP and the conventional grading capacitor pattern (CGCP) were conducted, and the maximum external electric field strength of the VI with SSCP was reduced by 53.6%, while the temperature rise was also decreased by 33.9%. A 40.5-kV VI prototype with SSCP was developed based on ring capacitors, external shields, and integrated encapsulation. Experimental results for series-connected VIs with SSCP demonstrate that the potential distributions among the shields and breaks approach the ideal values. The withstand voltage of series-connected VIs with SSCP is increased by 12.5%, and the temperature rise is decreased by 32.2%. The feasibility of the VI with SSCP has been verified, providing a compact voltage-sharing design reference for ultra-high-voltage multi-break VCBs in GIS.

title: Discrimination of Tree-Contact High-Impedance and Flame Faults in Distribution Networks via Zero-Sequence Voltage Monitoring
abstract: Tree-contact high-impedance faults (THIF) and flame faults are common fault types in the forest area. Their mitigation and prevention are crucial to the management of distribution network faults. However, the signals of these faults are so weak that existing zero-sequence protection methods cannot ensure effectiveness and accuracy during the early fault stage. To address this issue, this paper investigates the electro-thermal coupling mechanism during the fault evolution process. Fault resistance models are established for different fault types. Experiments on 10 kV and 35 kV distribution systems verify that the proposed models can effectively capture the time-varying characteristics of the faults. Then electrical characteristics are investigated during discharges by applying Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to the zero-sequence voltage. Feature parameters are obtained including Total Harmonic Distortion (THD), Power Spectral Entropy (PSE), Skewness (SKE) and Kurtosis (KUR) of the sub-fundamental spectral components. Statistical analysis is employed to mitigate the influence of individual sample variability. From the experimental results, the frequency domain characteristics of both THIF and flame faults are independent of voltage levels. THD of flame fault is significantly higher than that of THIF due to the unstable discharge path in the flame. Conversely, THIF shows higher SKE and KUR because of low-frequency turbulence in the flame. The combined unstable discharge channel and turbulence cause PSE to be significantly higher in flame fault than in THIF. This research provides a methodological basis for fault classification and prevention for both 10 kV and 35 kV distribution lines.

title: Quantitative Metrics for Evaluating Grid Strength Across Power System Stability Domains: A Review
abstract: The increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is reducing grid strength, making accurate assessment essential for reliable and stable power system operation. Quantitative metrics offer systematic and practical tools for evaluating grid strength, supporting both planning and operational decisions. This paper provides a comprehensive review of quantitative metrics for grid strength assessment across static, small-signal, and transient stability domains. Metrics are categorized and discussed in terms of their definitions, derivation methods, advantages, and limitations, with particular attention to the effects of IBR interactions, network topology, and control strategies. Relevant stability criteria, practical applicability, and recommended threshold values are also summarized. This review aims to support system planners and operators in selecting and applying appropriate grid strength metrics in power systems with high IBR penetration.

title: Thermomechanical Modeling of Clamping Forces in Power Transformers With Field Data Validation
abstract: Maintaining the mechanical integrity of a power transformer during large fault currents requires a clamping system that exerts sufficient compressive forces on the windings. This paper presents a thermomechanical model for the clamping force in a power transformer. The model predicts changes in clamping forces due to operating conditions, such as load and ambient temperatures, to indicate when the transformer is most vulnerable to mechanical failures. The model was tested and evaluated on one year of operational data collected from a 40 MVA ONAN transformer equipped with extensive temperature monitoring and novel clamping force sensors. By using only transformer design data, fundamental material parameters and results from the heat run test, the model was able to replicate the general trends observed in the measured clamping force. The model was able to predict the daily mean clamping force throughout the year with a mean absolute error of 6.6 kN, which corresponds to 2.9% of the initial clamping force at the start of the year. For daily variations, i.e., the difference between maximum and minimum clamping force for each day, the model was able to predict variations with a mean error of 2.1 kN. However, the model overestimates the changes in clamping force, as it is too sensitive to changes in loading and ambient temperature.

title: Research on the Diagnosis and Localization Method of Cross-Bonding Cable Defects Based on Three-Phase Differential Frequency Excitation
abstract: In high-voltage network, long-distance cables use cross bonding (CB) to eliminate the sheath currents and ensure the stable operation of the power system. Existing impedance testing suffers from signal attenuation and distortion due to limited instrument output, while cross-bonding causes phase coupling and signal aliasing, which interfere with defect diagnosis and localization accuracy. These combined factors affect the accuracy of defect localization for the cables. This paper proposes a method for diagnosing and locating defects in cross-bonding cables based on three-phase differential frequency excitation. An equivalent CB cable model was constructed to analyze the relationship between defects and resonant frequency shifts. A CB cable impedance spectrum analysis method was constructed, utilizing small frequency differences and fundamental frequency information to achieve full coverage of defect information for three single-phase cables in the wide frequency range. A testing system is built to obtain impedance spectra for damaged and thermally aged cables. Based on the offset characteristics of peak frequencies, the identification of defect types was achieved. Defect types are identified based on peak frequency offsets, and a differential frequency localization function is used to locate defects with an accuracy of 0.1%, verifying the effectiveness of the method.

title: Critical End-Effect at Sea-to-Land Transition of Three Core Submarine Cables
abstract: At the sea-to-land transition or offshore interfaces, three-core submarine cables are separated into individual single-core cables arranged in a flat configuration. This separation, combined with protective layers over metallic sheaths that impart semiconductive properties and cause spatial bonding, results in localized increases in circulating sheath currents in the submarine portion of the installation. Despite potential thermal consequences in offshore cable projects, this specific issue has received limited attention in the existing literature; consequently, this paper presents a novel examination of this end-effect phenomenon. An analytical model is developed in the paper and cross-validated with a comprehensive three-dimensional Finite Element Method (FEM) model and PI-section simulations, which represent fundamentally different approaches. The analysis reveals that sheath circulating currents in the sea-to-land transition section increased by a factor of up to 1.8 compared to the undisturbed three-core submarine cable configuration. This increase caused the maximum conductor temperatures to exceed 100 °C, far more than the 90 °C operational limit for XLPE insulation. The study addresses practical mitigation strategies for end effects in submarine cable installations and addresses a critical gap in existing methods for rating calculations of submarine power cables.

title: Sequential Switching Modeling and Transient Instability Mechanism for MMC-HVDC Receiving-End Systems With Fault Ride-Through
abstract: Previous literature shows that the second-order phase-locked loop dynamics dominate the transient stability of high voltage direct current system based on modular multilevel converter (MMC-HVDC) in the during-fault stage. The effects of DC-link dynamics and transient behavior after fault recovery have rarely been studied. Focusing on the post-fault stage, this paper first develops a transient model in each fault stage based on the typical fault ride-through strategy, considering the DC-link voltage dynamics. Although the during-fault stage is stable, the MMC-HVDC system still faces the risk of transient instability in the post-fault stage under receiving-end AC weak grid faults because of DC voltage deviation. The angular frequency jumps that occur in both the during-fault stage and post-fault stage are uncovered. High-dimensional basin-of-attraction analysis reveals that the angular frequency jump generated by the DC-link voltage dynamics can weaken the resynchronization capability. Moreover, based on the proposed transient stability margin index, the parameter feasible region under different ramp coefficients, DC voltage droop coefficients, and short circuit ratios is obtained. Finally, hardware-in-the-loop experiments are conducted to validate the results of the theoretical analysis.

title: Analysis of Lightning-Elevated Structures Interaction in Tropical Regions and Implications for Wind Turbine Risk Assessment
abstract: This study analyzes the lightning interaction with elevated structures (ES) in a high-lightning activity region of central Colombia by integrating Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) observations with LINET cloud-to-ground stroke data. In addition, the annual number of lightning flashes (<inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) to ES is determined directly from LINET measurements and compared with the obtain using the expression of NTC 4552-2:2023, IEC 62305-2:2024, and the Eriksson equation. The same analysis is extended to two wind farms in northern Colombia, where <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula> for wind turbines is evaluated following the IEC 61400-24:2018 standard. LMA observations show that all CG strokes affecting ES are initiated by downward leaders and influenced by the lower positive charge region (LPCR) in thunderstorms. Likewise, positive leaders exhibited significantly longer paths than negative leaders. Analysis of <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula> reveals two exposure regimes: in low-activity regions, structural height governs <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula>, whereas in high-activity zones the ground flash density (<inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_G}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) becomes the dominant factor, particularly for ES below 70 m. In general, the <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula> values obtained from LINET exceed those predicted by the normative formulations. However, using ground strike-point density (<inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_G}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) values derived directly from the lightning location system (LLS) substantially improves the agreement between calculated and observed <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${{N}_D}$</tex-math></inline-formula> values, particularly for tall structures and wind turbines, thereby avoiding the underestimation of lightning-related design parameters such as the risk components.

title: Line Equivalent Based Short-Circuit Current Calculation in Distribution Networks With Numerous Inverter Interfaced Distributed Generators
abstract: The calculation of short-circuit current (SCC) is crucial for planning, operation and maintenance of distribution systems. The integration of Inverter-Interfaced Distributed Generators (IIDGs) into distribution systems induces nonlinear characteristics, which make the traditional nodal voltage equation-based SCC calculation methods ineffective. To balance the SCC calculation accuracy and efficiency, a line equivalent based SCC calculation method is proposed to address the increasing integration of IIDGs in distribution networks. Firstly, an aggregation zoning method for IIDGs is proposed based on their fault response characteristics. Both the Low Voltage Ride Through (LVRT) controlling and fault steady-state voltage drop are considered. Then, an equivalent model of the non-fault line, utilizing piecewise equivalence, is established to simplify the network structure. Finally, the post-fault node voltages and branch currents are determined by solving the nodal voltage equation of the established simplified network with fixed-point iteration. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed algorithm has satisfactory accuracy and computation time in calculating SCC of distribution networks with numerous IIDGs.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Objective Design of Lightning Protection for Complex Power Distribution Networks
abstract: Some of the main issues in developing an effective lightning protection strategy include determining the optimal placement of protection devices and deciding whether to incorporate shield wires. Addressing these challenges involves balancing multiple, often conflicting, objectives. Additionally, the intrinsic probabilistic nature of the lightning problem makes the optimization even more complicated. Based on the above considerations, this study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework to identify effective lightning protection strategies, in terms of surge arrester location and shield wire installation in complex distribution networks. The proposed approach aims to find a computationally efficient procedure that preserves the accuracy of conventional methods, even in complex network configurations. This is accomplished by integrating decision theory with a Design of Experiments approach based on Taguchi arrays to determine the optimal protection alternative. This method allows obtaining substantial reduction of the computational time. The computational time reduction depends on the network complexity and on the configuration of the reference method. In the simulations presented in this paper, the proposed approach allowed reducing computational time up to approximately 98% compared to a benchmark method based on genetic algorithm combined with the Monte Carlo technique, while preserving the accuracy of the results. The proposed method offers a practical and scalable solution for enhancing lightning resilience despite the complexity of the distribution networks' topology.

title: A Unified Probability Model for Multi-Type Power Quality Disturbances Based on Operating States Identification
abstract: The Grid-connected inverter (GCI) inevitably generates the multi-type power quality disturbances at the same time; for example, it not only emits harmonic currents but also causes voltage fluctuations. Building one model to describe the multi-type disturbances is necessary for disturbance source tracing, disturbance prediction, mitigation decision, and so on. This study proposes a unified probability model for multi-type power quality disturbances for GCI based on operating states identification. Firstly, it proposes an operating states identification algorithm considering multi-type disturbances, to facilitate the construction of the disturbance model for different operating states. Secondly, the unified probability model for multi-type power quality disturbances is developed, which includes the edge probability model and unified probability model, to analyze the occurrence probability and coupling relationship of multi-type disturbances. Finally, the accuracy and validity of the proposed method are verified by using the real recorded data of photovoltaic (PV) GCI in practice.

title: Different-Frequency Differential Protection Method of Adjustable Speed Hydro-Generating Unit Based on Fixed Characteristic Frequency Band
abstract: During the operation of Adjustable speed hydro-generating unit (ASHU), due to high speed and large centrifugal force, the rotor winding is easily squeezed and causes short-circuit fault. The development of a reliable protection scheme is imperative. As a new and potential method, the universality of different-frequency differential protection is still limited under wide speed operation conditions. Therefore, a rotor winding short-circuit protection method based on fixed characteristic frequency band is proposed in this paper. Firstly, the internal relationship between the harmonic characteristics of rotor current and slip rate in the case of winding short-circuit fault of ASHU is analyzed. On this basis, the construction method of different-frequency differential current protection criterion based on fixed characteristic frequency band is proposed. Furthermore, combined with the waveform of the dynamic simulation experiment, the Generalized S Transform (GST) is used to carry out time-frequency analysis. The feasibility of the construction approach of the protection criterion is verified. Finally, the experimental results show that the proposed protection method is suitable for the wide speed operation condition of ASHU. It can achieve fast action under rotor winding short-circuit fault (RWSF), and has high selectivity under stator winding short-circuit fault (SWSF), which can effectively avoid protection misoperation.

title: Hybrid Grid-Forming Control for Enhanced Active Support and DC Voltage Stability in MMC-HVDC Systems
abstract: Grid-forming control based on power synchronization and DC voltage synchronization is two typical approaches for enabling modular multilevel converter-based high-voltage direct current (MMC-HVDC) systems to operate in weak grids. However, the inherent limitations of their synchronization mechanisms make it difficult to simultaneously ensure system stability and economic efficiency. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a two-stage hybrid grid-forming control strategy. In the first stage, a decoupled matching control is designed to exploit the energy stored in submodule (SM) capacitors for active damping support, which achieves nonlinear indirect matching between DC voltage and frequency while maintaining the economic operation of the sending-end grid. Meanwhile, a voltage stabilization method based on redundant SMs is proposed to decouple SM capacitor voltage from the DC voltage, thereby enhancing DC voltage stability. In the second stage, once the average voltage of the SMs exceeds a predefined threshold, virtual synchronous generator control mobilizes the reserved energy from renewable plants and the rotor kinetic energy of wind turbines, further strengthening inertia and damping support. Moreover, a small-signal model is developed to reveal the parameter evolution, and a unified two-stage framework is established through control correction and parameter optimization, thereby improving system dynamic performance and stability. Finally, PSCAD/EMTDC simulations validate the correctness and effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Quasi-Steady-State Frequency Based ROCOF Relay Realisation for Secured LOM Protection
abstract: Rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) relay is widely used to detect loss of main (LoM) events. RoCoF is commonly calculated using the frequency estimated through phase-locked loop (PLL). These relays monitor the RoCoF and initiate tripping when predefined thresholds are exceeded. However, PLL-based frequency estimators are prone to producing erroneous RoCoF measurements during transient system conditions, leading to unnecessary source disconnection despite the system remaining within ride-through limits. This paper uses the concept of a geometric definition of frequency to calculate RoCoF and assert its validity during transients. The proposed logic can help in improving the security of the RoCoF relay and prevent undesired tripping of distributed generation compared to PLL based logic.

title: Sinusoidality Index
abstract: Maintaining sinusoidal or near-sinusoidal operating conditions in electrical systems is essential, as is their accurate assessment. This letter proposes a novel metric, namely the sinusoidality index, which quantifies the instantaneous deviation of the trajectory of an ac voltage vector with respect to a circle under any periodic operating conditions. This metric differs from conventional Fourier-based estimations by accounting for the trajectory of the waveform rather than its spectral decomposition. A variety of examples illustrates the properties of the proposed metric and highlights insights that may not be captured by conventional approaches.

title: Multiple Regulation Phase Shifting Transformer: A Flexible and High-Accuracy Power Flow Controller
abstract: With the increasing share of renewable energy in modern power systems, the power grid urgently needs effective power flow regulation technology. The phase shifting transformer has the advantages of strong power flow regulation capability, low investment, high reliability, but the traditional phase shifting transformer can only realize discrete regulation, with low regulation accuracy and lack of appropriate amplitude regulation capability. Therefore, this paper proposes a multiple regulating phase shifting transformer (MR-PST) and its design scheme for power system, analyzes its input and output characteristics based on its topology, examines the nature and distribution of its compensation voltage, and establishes boundary equations from the constraints of single amplitude regulation and dual phase regulation, proving that this structure can effectively increase the number of regulation points, increase the regulation accuracy, introduce the amplitude regulation capability, and optimize the regulation region. Then the power flow regulation region is quantitatively analyzed, and the extremum expression and boundary calculation method of power flow regulation range under different conditions are obtained. Finally, the rationality and practicality of MR-PST were verified through virtual simulation and physical experiments.

title: A Physics-Informed Topology-Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network for Harmonic Source Location in Three-Phase Distribution Networks With Renewable Energy Integration
abstract: The large-scale integration of renewable energy sources has led to a significant increase in the number of harmonic sources within distribution networks. Concurrently, the altered supply modes introduced by renewable integration have caused dynamic changes in the network topology. Therefore, this paper proposes a three-phase distribution network harmonic source location method based on a physics-informed topology adaptive graph convolutional network. Firstly, a harmonic pseudo-measurement method based on emission characteristics modelling is developed to address the shortage of harmonic measurements. Secondly, considering the dynamic changes in the distribution network topology, a multi-layer perception topology adaptive graph convolutional neural network is proposed, which is used to establish the mapping relationship between harmonic measurements and state variables. Meanwhile, the harmonic transfer equation and system parameters are embedded into the neural network training as physical constraints to ensure the results conform to physical properties. Then, a harmonic source identification criterion is established, and the long-term statistical index derived from the estimated harmonic injection current is used to locate harmonic sources in the distribution network. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed method was verified in the IEEE 37-bus system and the actual system.

title: Impedance-Spectrum Driven Frequency-Weighted Functional Fault Location in Undersea Observation Network Power Systems
abstract: Fault location in the power supply systems of undersea observation networks is constrained by limited observability and the frequency-dependent characteristics of the electrode–seawater–cable loop. This paper proposes a frequency-domain fault location method based on impedance spectrum analysis, in which the identification of fault parameters is formulated as a minimization problem of a frequency-weighted residual functional. A physical model of the electrode–cable–fault path is constructed to compute theoretical input impedance spectra under different fault distances and fault impedances. These spectra are then compared to the measured impedance spectrum obtained at the shore station under swept-frequency excitation. The residual functional is constructed by separating the real and imaginary components of the spectral difference, reflecting the deviation of complex input impedance at each frequency point. Considering the influence of impedance sensitivity across frequencies, independent weighting functions are introduced for the real and imaginary components to enhance contributions from informative bands and suppress unreliable regions. This yields a frequency-weighted residual functional with physical significance, characterizing the correspondence between fault parameters and spectral discrepancy. The functional is minimized via a gradient-based optimization strategy, enabling simultaneous determination of fault distance and fault impedance based solely on shore-side measurements. Simulation studies across various fault conditions validate the method's performance in terms of location accuracy, robustness under high impedance scenarios, and numerical stability over long transmission distances. The proposed framework fuses spectral sensitivity with physical transmission modeling to infer spatial fault characteristics solely from frequency-domain observations, without relying on internal measurements or reflectometry.

title: Transient Voltage and Current Calculations Based on Formulation of Modified Baum-Liu-Tesche Equation in Phase Domain
abstract: This study presents a modified Baum-Liu-Tesche (BLT) equation, derived in a compact matrix-algebraic form, for the frequency-domain analysis of transient voltages and currents in multi-conductor transmission lines (MTLs). The proposed formulation addresses two broad categories of transient events, including faults and lightning strikes, while accommodating diverse event types and occurrence scenarios. The modified BLT equation is further extended into an explicit form, enabling its application to power networks with inhomogeneous parameters and complex topologies. This extension is supported by a systematic derivation of the structural features and element characteristics of the involved matrices and vectors. Numerical validation using the benchmark IEEE 34-bus test distribution network confirms strong agreement between the results obtained from the modified BLT equation and those generated by electromagnetic-transient-type simulations. Overall, the proposed formulation provides an effective and robust analytical framework for transient analysis in power systems.

title: Contour Optimization of DC-GIS Insulator Considering the Influence of Surface Charging Withstanding Transient Voltages
abstract: Surface charging on insulator in DC-GIS is influenced by transient voltages like lightning impulse (LI) and polarity reversal (PR), which threatens the safe operation of the equipment. In this paper, a contour optimization method considering the influence of surface charging is proposed for insulator used in DC-GIS of ±320 kV. The insulation reliability under steady DC voltage is promoted, and the property to withstand the transient voltages is guaranteed as well. The normal and tangential components of electric field under steady DC voltage are simultaneously minimized, and the constraints on electric field under the transient voltages are incorporated. The results show that, under the steady DC voltage, the maximal value of normal electric field is reduced by 5.8%, and the tangential field is simultaneously reduced by 7.0% on the insulator with the optimal contour after optimization. The maximal values of electric fields under the LI and PR voltages are 8.82 and 3.49 kV/mm, respectively, meeting the insulation requirements. It is suggested that, the proposed method incorporating the property withstanding the LI and PR voltages yields a more reliable performance of the optimized insulator in DC-GIS.

title: Effect of IBR Negative-Sequence Control on Phase-to-Phase Fault Direction Determination
abstract: Protective relays implement algorithms to determine the direction to the fault. Phase-to-phase fault detection, can rely on negative sequence components. If the negative sequence currents provided by an inverter-based resource (IBR) are not reliable, the directional determination of the fault is not consistent. In this paper, we compare two types of IBRs: grid-following (GFL) and grid-forming (GFM), for their dynamic performance when subject to phase-to-phase faults on the high side of the step-up transformer. The GFL-IBR behaves as a positive-sequence current source, while the GFM-IBR behaves as a voltage source behind an inductive impedance in the positive-sequence circuit, and as an inductive impedance in the negative-sequence circuit. It is found that the GFM-IBR ensures proper fault ride-through, while the GFL-IBR cannot ride through such a fault. Additionally, the GFM-IBR ensures correct fault detection via negative-sequence directionality check, while this check fails for the GFL-IBR case. Therefore, the GFM design presented in this paper appears to have two advantages compared to the legacy GFL design: better capability of fault ride-through and assurance of correct fault direction determination.

title: Vibration-Based Detection of Cable Bending in Cable GIS Terminations via Experimental Measurements and Interface Stress Simulation
abstract: Cable GIS terminations are prone to insulation defects induced by abnormal internal stress and strain, due to their complex internal structure, latent defects, and sensitivity to installation quality. One typical manifestation of such abnormal mechanical states is internal cable bending, whose influence on the vibration response of cable GIS terminations remains insufficiently understood. To address this issue, this study proposes a vibration-based method for detecting abnormal stress-strain conditions at insulation interfaces, enabling early identification of hidden insulation defects. First, vibration theory and simulation models are combined to examine how internal cable bending influences interfacial insulation pressure and the corresponding vibration response. Subsequently, a vibration testing platform for 110-kV cable GIS terminations is established to measure and analyze the vibration characteristics under normal and simulated abnormal stress-strain conditions, with the latter induced by cable bending. Finally, the vibration characteristics are evaluated using time-domain and frequency-domain indicators. The results demonstrate that internal cable bending leads to non-uniform stress distributions at the insulation interfaces between the bushing, stress cone, and cable. The cable-end vibration, which is typically the most pronounced under normal conditions, is significantly suppressed, accompanied by a noticeable shift of the vibration signal toward the lower-frequency domain and an increase in damping. These findings establish a vibration response characterization framework for cable bending defects and provide a basis for non-intrusive condition assessment of cable GIS terminations.

title: Fault Analysis and Pilot Protection Scheme for Various Single-Phase Line Breaks in Resonant Grounding Systems
abstract: Due to small fault currents and different fault characteristics under various grounding types on both sides of the fault point, the existing methods are facing challenges in the analysis and protection principle for single-phase break faults (SPBFs) in resonant grounding systems (RGSs), including inaccurate fault identification, low sensitivity, and insufficient reliability under high-impedance grounding and intermittent arc faults. In this paper, fault characteristics of zero-sequence voltages upstream and downstream of the break point with different grounding modes are analyzed. The SPBFs with grounding at single-side and without grounding only exhibit the amplitude or phase characteristic, while SPBFs with grounding at both sides incorporate the two features. On this basis, a pilot protection scheme is developed for various SPBFs in RGSs, where internal and external SPBFs are determined by combining the features of the amplitude and phase of dual-terminal zero-sequence voltages. The effectiveness of the proposed methodology is validated through a closed-loop hardware test by applying a real-time digital simulator (RTDS) and the developed protective devices. Experimental results prove that the protection scheme performs well under different fault types, fault locations, fault resistances, and the presence of inverter-interfaced distributed generators.

title: Degradation, Lifetime, and Failure Modes of Metal Oxide Varistors in Low-Voltage DC Circuit Breaker Applications
abstract: The metal oxide varistor (MOV) has been a critical enabling component for emerging applications in low-voltage dc circuit breakers (LVDCCBs). Although its properties align well with this application, its long-term performance, including degradation, failure modes, and service lifetime, remains poorly understood. Based on an accelerated degradation test (ADT) platform, this work collects extensive data to track degradation patterns and identify failure modes using statistical methods. A power-function-based model is proposed to identify the driving forces behind degradation, and a complete lifetime map of LVDCCB MOVs is achieved. The model predicts the lifetime of LVDCCB MOVs with a confidence level of 79.18%. The model and statistical analysis indicate that charge is the driving force for the defined failure mode, which needs to be addressed in the LVDCCB design while energy drives the catastrophic failure mode, which needs to be avoided in the LVDCCB design.

title: Investigation of the External Thermal Resistance of Cables in Backfills and Duct Banks
abstract: The Neher/McGrath paper and IEC Standard 60287-2-1 provide formulas for calculating the external thermal resistance of cables installed in backfills or duct banks. In this context, the backfill or duct bank is represented as a circular isothermal surface, assuming that the thermal resistances of both are equivalent. The 2023 edition of IEC Standard 60287-2-1 introduces a table of geometric factors to calculate the radius of the equivalent circle. In contrast, earlier editions relied on an analytical formula that assumed the backfill's width-to-height ratio was between 1/3 and 3. This paper investigates modeling problems arising from the application of the new IEC standard 60287-2-1 to cables installed in duct banks and backfills. The findings indicate that assumptions in the IEC standard for modeling the external thermal resistance of cables may lead to significant errors. As a result, the paper proposes a new approach that addresses weaknesses in the standard approach. The new approach is verified through a finite-element analysis. Several numerical examples illustrate the differences between the proposed approach and the results based on the standard analysis.

title: Transient Voltage Stability Analysis and Enhancement of Grid-Following Converters Considering DC-link Voltage Control Dynamics
abstract: With the large-scale integration of renewable energy resources through grid-following converters, the voltage support capability of the system is weakened, thereby increasing the risk of voltage instability. Existing studies mainly focus on the transient voltage stability of induction motors (IMs), where the dynamics of voltage source converters (VSCs) are often neglected. However, VSCs with DC-link voltage control (DVC) also face the risk of transient voltage instability under grid faults, even when the voltage-supporting effect of VSCs during low-voltage ride through (LVRT) is considered. Such an instability phenomenon poses a tremendous threat to the stable operation of VSC-dominated power systems, which has not been addressed in existing research. To fill this gap, this paper provides a theoretical explanation of the VSC’s transient performance under DVC and LVRT, and reveals the transient voltage instability mechanism of modern power systems with high penetration of VSCs. To mitigate such instability, this paper proposes an adaptive current-limiting control strategy after analyzing the impact of current limitation on transient voltage stability. Simulation results verify the correctness of the theoretical analysis and the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy.

title: Assessing Emission Limits in the Supraharmonic 20 to150 kHz Range
Fully Actuated Control of Point-to-Point VSC–HVDC Links for Frequency and DC Voltage Regulation in Asynchronous AC Systems
abstract: Grid-forming (GFM) VSC–HVDC systems can provide frequency support to ac grids, particularly in point-to-point VSC–HVDC links interconnecting asynchronous ac systems. However, large power variations commanded for frequency support may jeopardize the dc-link voltage stability. To simultaneously enhance frequency support and preserve dc-link voltage regulation, this paper develops two robust controllers for the rectifier and inverter stations based on the fully actuated control (FAC) theory. FAC provides a systematic diffeomorphism-based transformation that converts the original under-actuated and strongly coupled station dynamics into an equivalent fully actuated form, thereby revealing virtual input channels and enabling direct shaping of the key dc-voltage- and frequency-related states for controller synthesis. In the transformed coordinates, multiple perturbations—including stochastic load variations, parameter uncertainties, and external disturbances—are aggregated as lumped disturbances. High-gain disturbance observers are then designed for both stations to estimate the lumped disturbances. Leveraging the observer-based estimates, a robust sliding-mode control law is formulated in the fully actuated coordinates to compensate the aggregated uncertainties, thereby ensuring resilient frequency support while maintaining dc-link voltage regulation. Simulation studies on two test systems validate the effectiveness of the proposed controllers in regulating the dc-link voltage and supporting grid frequency under multiple scenarios.

title: A Constrained Formulation for Simultaneous Line Parameter Estimation and Instrument Transformer Calibration
abstract: The process of calibrating instrument transformers (ITs) has been greatly simplified by using phasor measurement unit (PMU) data since this process eliminates the need for (a) additional hardware, and (b) taking ITs offline. However, such simplification comes at the cost of knowing the line parameters, whose estimation using PMU data in turn requires calibrated ITs. To solve this interdependency problem, we propose a novel framework that incorporates power system domain knowledge as constraints to perform simultaneous line parameter estimation and IT calibration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with simulated and real PMU data as well as for a power system application that uses both PMU data and line parameter information.

title: Analysis of Electric Field Shielding Characteristics on Residential Platforms and Optimization of Shielding Position Near 1000 kV Double-Circuit Transmission Lines on the Same Tower
abstract: The electric field strength beneath 1000 kV ultra-high-voltage transmission lines is relatively high, posing a risk of excessive electric field exposure in the presence of nearby buildings. Shielding wires are an effective technical measure to mitigate excessive electric field strength at sensitive locations; however, optimal performance depends on the appropriate selection of shielding parameters such as wire size and placement. In this study, a 6 m × 6 m building platform was constructed beneath a 1000 kV double-circuit transmission line mounted on a single tower. Shielding wires with heights of 5 m, 6 m, and 7 m were installed. The electric field distribution above the building, as well as the shielding effects, were analyzed. The optimal positioning of the shielding wires was also investigated. The results indicate that the electric field on the upper surface of the platform closest to the transmission line side can reach 5 kV/m, while the electric field on the second-level platform can reach up to 7.5 kV/m. A single shielding wire can reduce the electric field strength by 21.7%, whereas multiple wires can achieve reductions of more than 30% . We convert the above electric field model into a mathematical model and propose an optimization method for the shielding wires position. When the height of the shielding wire is less than 8 m, the optimal placement is approximately directly above the sensitive point. These findings provide practical guidance for mitigating electric fields near sensitive areas and offer a technical foundation for the design and installation of shielding wires.

title: Prior Knowledge-Guided Active Learning Network for Multi-Source Partial Discharge Diagnosis in Gas-Insulated Switchgear
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence presents both opportunities and significant challenges for multi-source partial discharge (PD) diagnosis in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS), but challenges remain due to insufficient incorporation of underlying physical mechanisms, limited labeled data, noise interference, class imbalance, and difficulties in decoupling mixed PD sources. To address these issues, this paper proposes a prior knowledge–guided active learning network (PKGALN) for multi-source PD diagnosis in GIS, in which physics-related PD characteristics are explicitly embedded into the model design under a limited-label regime. Specifically, a prior knowledge–guided U-former is constructed by incorporating physically interpretable PD descriptors (e.g., time–frequency statistical features reflecting discharge behavior) as global guidance for feature learning, while a scale-guided convolutional–wavelet encoder enhances denoising and multi-scale representation capability. In addition, a multi-label decoupling recognition module is designed to explicitly handle mixed PD sources, and a distribution-balanced loss is adopted to alleviate severe class imbalance. To further reduce annotation cost, an adaptive active learning strategy is introduced, dynamically balancing uncertainty and diversity during sample selection. Experimental results on both laboratory and field datasets demonstrate that PKGALN achieves diagnostic accuracies of 96.39% and 93.26%, respectively, using only 10% of labeled samples. By leveraging limited labeled data, the proposed approach enables robust diagnosis of both single-source and multi-source PDs.

title: Nonintrusive Distributed Detection Method for GIS Metal Particle Defects Based on a ϕ-OTDR
A Hybrid Multi-Agent Fault Location Strategy in Active Distribution Network Using Synchrophasors
abstract: Locating faults and isolating the faulted sections of the network are integral to the smooth operation of any self-healing distribution system. A novel multi-agent system based event location and isolation approach is proposed for a modern power distribution system using synchronized current and voltage from a limited number of PMUs. The developed multi-agent framework uses a decentralized hierarchical agent scheme and consists of heterogeneous agent types, with the PMUs defined as the main computational agents. The agents receive their local synchrophasor measurements and perform the algorithm by communicating with their neighboring agents to locate the faulted bus with minimal communication messages. The new fault location algorithm is a two-step process: first, the agents identify the faulted section using impedance comparison and isolate the faulted zone; second, the corresponding agents within the zone identify the faulted bus using voltage comparison and send the bus information to the control center. Studies are conducted by interconnecting the IEEE 34-bus network with distributed energy resources developed in PSCAD/EMTDC and a multi-agent system implemented on the JADE platform. Simulations of various test cases verify the efficacy of the proposed multi-agent scheme in accurately locating various faults occurring in the distribution network.

title: Molecularly engineered zwitterionic‑fluorinated hydrogel electrolyte for durable Ah-level zinc-ion batteries
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries are considered suitable candidates for grid storage but suffer from Zn dendrites and water-induced side reactions. Incorporating appropriate hydrophobic moieties into hydrogel electrolytes is an effective strategy to reduce water activity and widen the electrochemical stability window. To further advance this molecular design framework and enable precise interphase modulation, we report a molecularly engineered zwitterionic-fluorinated hydrogel electrolyte. Within the polymer network, the rationally introduced hydrophobic fluoroalkyl moieties (–CH2CF3) strengthen hydrogen bonds between hydrophilic units and water, thereby reducing water activity and mitigating parasitic reactions. Meanwhile, the zincophilic zwitterionic units (–SO3–, –N+(CH3)3) facilitate rapid and directional Zn2+ transport, with a Zn2+ transference number of 0.76. These tailored functional groups synergistically promote the in-situ formation of an organic–inorganic solid electrolyte interphase, enabling Zn negative electrode stability, achieving over 900 h of Zn plating/stripping at 5.0 mA cm–2 and 5.0 mAh cm–2. Furthermore, Zn | |MnO2 pouch cells incorporating this electrolyte deliver a capacity of ~1 Ah and operate for over 700 h, indicating the potential of this electrolyte for large-scale energy storage applications.

title: Head-to-tail assembled borphyrins for solid-state lithium extraction
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Lithium is a critical mineral for advancing greener technologies. Extraction of lithium ions (Li⁺) from sea salt, minerals, and waste is important, but has been hindered by the lack of extraction methods that offer both high selectivity and strong lithium affinity. Here, we report a dioxaborole-linked, head-to-tail assembled macrocycle – termed borphyrin – featuring a rigid cavity with a 16-crown-4-like configuration. This molecule exhibits strong affinity for lithium and high selectivity over competing cations under dry solid-liquid extraction conditions, owing to its narrow binding cavity and planar macrocyclic core. Borphyrin enabled the extraction of lithium from crystalline solids of ether-insoluble salts, as well as selective extraction of Li⁺ from dried mixed-salt matrices containing alkali, alkaline earth and transition-metal salts. These results establish borphyrin as a potential molecular platform for selective lithium recognition and solid-liquid lithium extraction.

title: Transmission Line Galloping Detection System Based on an Improved PIDNet
abstract: The galloping phenomenon of transmission lines, exacerbated by extreme weather, poses a significant threat to grid stability and power supply. The practical application of conventional sensor-based methods is limited by high deployment costs and low adaptability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an end-to-end galloping detection system based on video monitoring. An improved PIDNet forms the segmentation backbone, incorporating a Line-features Interactive Two-Branch (LITB) network to leverage line orientation priors, a Detail Recovery Decoder (DRD) to enhance line continuity, and an Edge Perception Module (EPM) to refine boundary segmentation against complex backgrounds. Optical flow analysis is subsequently employed to quantify transmission line displacement and determine galloping states. Experimental results demonstrate performance improvements of 6.9% in mIoU, 4.23% in mAcc, and 4.8% mDice over popular segmentation models. The proposed embedded detection system achieves an accuracy of 84.00%, a recall of 90.31%, and an F1-score of 87.17% when deployed on edge devices.
